To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

our genetic map of MS susceptibility includes 233 independent associations that are genome wide statistically significant and 416 additional associations that have suggestive evidence of replication, together explaining ~48% of MS heritability.

the genetics of MS implicates multiple immune cell types, including brain resident microglia, in the onset of MS and that these cells may be the targets for the development of primary prevention strategies for MS.
we have generated a comprehensive genetic map of multiple sclerosis (MS), which includes the first susceptibility variant on a sex chromosome.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the genetic basis of MS and how it leads to an inflammatory and degenerate disease of the brain.
identifying the genetic architecture of the disease, understanding the biological mechanisms that underlie the genetic risk, and using this knowledge to develop primary prevention strategies.
identifying the genes that are responsible for susceptibility to multiple sclerosis (MS).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
MS is a disease that is caused by the interplay between multiple immune cell types, and that microglia are a key component of the process.
the genetics of MS is a complex story that implicates multiple different cell types and pathways.
MS is an immune mediated disease in which the genetic contribution of the disease is largely driven by immune cells of the adaptive arm and, perhaps, the innate arm.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the MS genetic architecture is complex and involves the peripheral and brain innate and adaptive immune systems.
we have established a detailed genetic and functional map of MS susceptibility that explains nearly half of this disease’s heritability.

the MS genetic map implicating microglia as an important component of the disease process, along with multiple different peripheral immune cells, and that this map sets the stage for a next generation of functional studies that will uncover the sequence of events leading to the onset of this devastating disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have identified a large number of genes that contribute to MS, many of which are involved in immune cell development, maturation and function.
we have identified the cells that are most likely involved in the initial events that trigger MS and that these cells can be targeted to prevent the onset of the disorder.

the MS genetic map is a rich resource to inform functional studies that can elucidate the sequence of events that trigger MS onset and that can be leveraged to develop primary prevention strategies for MS.
